{"decisions": [
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D2","problem":"How to present experimental results so that others can judge whether the measurement and effect are sound.","did":"Always include the prompt beside the plot, truncating long prompts and putting the full version at the back of the slides.","alternatives_named":["showing only high-level conclusions"],"stated_reason":"The prompt describes how the metric in the chart is measured, and people in the meeting should be able to critique the experiment using the raw ingredients.","quote":"Always include your prompt. The prompt should describe how you are measuring your metric in the chart. Prompts are often long, so you can truncate the prompt and put the full version at the back of your slides."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D3","problem":"How to tell whether an observed difference in a proportion metric is real or just noise from a small sample.","did":"Show error bars, using standard error SE=sqrt(p(1-p)/N) times 1.96 as a fast heuristic for 95% intervals, while noting other sources of variance.","alternatives_named":["more rigorous error calculation methods"],"stated_reason":"Your mentor wants to know whether you ruled out simple things like getting lucky with 10 samples.","quote":"Show error bars. Your mentor wants to know whether you ruled out simple things like getting lucky with 10 samples. We use the standard error as a fast heuristic for proportion metrics."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D6","problem":"How to avoid presenting conclusions that may be wrong without letting others check the evidence.","did":"Put the raw ingredients (prompts, error bars) in the slides rather than only the conclusions drawn, so that others can critique the experiment.","alternatives_named":["presenting only high-level conclusions"],"stated_reason":"The conclusions you draw might be wrong, and you want people in the meeting to critique the experiment.","quote":"Part of the reason for showing the prompt and error bars is that you want people in the meeting to critique the experiment. So you want to have the “raw ingredients” in the slides, not just the high-level conclusions you are drawing (which might be wrong)."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D2","problem":"Which comparison conditions to include in a bar chart to show an intervention's effect.","did":"Use bars for the model before the intervention, a control baseline, and the model after the intervention, with at most 3 model types per slide.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"These are the typical comparisons needed to interpret the intervention's effect.","quote":"Rule of thumb — 3-5 colors max on a bar chart. These bars typically represent “model before your intervention”, “a control baseline”, and “model after your intervention”."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D2","problem":"How to respond when an intervention such as training on a dataset appears not to help.","did":"Be ready with a data-scaling plot (or a simple bar plot like 1k vs 20k) showing whether more data helps.","alternatives_named":["answering only with the single training run"],"stated_reason":"A common question is whether you have tried more data, and you should be able to answer it.","quote":"Suppose you try to intervene on a model by training on a dataset. And your training does not seem to help. One common question is “have you tried… more data?.” You should be ready to answer at that!"},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D1","problem":"How to look for regularities in results that help forecast model behavior.","did":"Try log-log plots and watch for scaling-law behavior, e.g. plotting -log(acc) on the y-axis when using accuracy.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Finding predictable scaling trends is helpful for forecasting.","quote":"Try log-log plots. Not always relevant, so use your judgment, but always keep an eye out for scaling law behavior (if using accuracy, try plotting -log(acc) on the y-axis). Finding predictable scaling trends is helpful for forecasting."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D3","problem":"How to guard against results that are produced by something simpler than the claimed effect.","did":"Think of simple baselines that would invalidate the results and include slides discussing them.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"","quote":"Proposed baselines. What are some simple ways that would invalidate your results? You should think of some and include slides that discuss it."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D5","problem":"How to treat a result that either worked or failed, since the interpretation determines the next experiments.","did":"State up front whether experiments worked, because a success calls for sanity checks, controls and extensions while a failure calls for debugging.","alternatives_named":["debugging by training with better data","improving the prompts"],"stated_reason":"The outcome sets the frame for what the mentor should think about next.","quote":"My experiments worked! Your mentor will focus on sanity checks, control experiments, and extensions to other setups.\n- My experiments didn’t work. Your mentor will focus on debugging why. E.g., train with better data, or improve the prompts."},
{"item_type":"rejected","point":"D2","problem":"Which of many tried experimental setups to show in the main results.","did":"Show only the best or most interesting setup first and move the other setups to backup slides rather than presenting all of them.","alternatives_named":["showing all 10 experimental setups","many bar charts on one slide"],"stated_reason":"Discussing many setups takes time, and often they didn't work and you have something better.","quote":"Even though you worked hard to try 10 different experimental setups, you don’t show all of them. Show your best setup first, or what your mentor would think is the most interesting."},
{"item_type":"rejected","point":"D2","problem":"What chart type to use to convey results clearly.","did":"Use simple charts such as bar charts and condense important results from heatmaps into a bar chart.","alternatives_named":["heatmaps","complicated charts"],"stated_reason":"Heatmaps require the audience to stare at both axes to find a value, which is tiring.","quote":"Heatmaps of values are hard to read. Heatmaps require the audience to stare at the y-axis and x-axis to find a particular value. This is tiring. Often you can condense the most important results into a bar chart."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D1","problem":"When to settle the framing of a paper's story relative to the experiments.","did":"Include slides in weekly meetings describing the current paper story and re-present it for feedback as results change.","alternatives_named":["leaving the story framing until late"],"stated_reason":"This makes it easier to write a paper that everyone is aligned on from the start.","quote":"Often getting the paper’s story and thinking about how you frame certain elements is left too late. We recommend including slides in your weekly meeting that describe the current story you want to tell so you can get feedback."},
{"item_type":"advice","point":"D2","problem":"How to decide what additional experiments or controls are needed after seeing results.","did":"Use the work of preparing slides to spot problems such as big error bars or missing controls and then fix them with more samples or new control setups.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Improving slides helped him iterate on experimental improvements.","quote":"The 1-2 days of improving slides helped me to iterate on experimental improvements. E.g. “It seems like my error bars are big here, I need more samples.” or “I’m missing a control setup here. I need to make one.”"}
]}
